The Scythians had reached Ciscaucasia 'between c. 750 and c. 700 BC', 'displaced the Agathyrsi and Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western steppe in the 8th century BC' and set their capital in the Kuban valley; in West Asia their 'power later centred on Sakez near Lake Urmia'. Same extent. Scyles pressed Nikonion, Tyras, Olbia and Kerkinitis (c. 460-450); about thirty colonies formed the Bosporan kingdom; stable relations with the Spartocids after c. 438 BCE. No border move.

region.text: the Kuban valley and Ciscaucasia, the kingdom's centre until c. 600 BC

'Between c. 680 and c. 677 BC, Esarhaddon struck deep into Median territory, and king Išpakāya was killed'; infobox Išpakaia 'unknown–679 BC', Bartatua '679–c. 665 BC'. The Scythians 'settled the Kuban valley and set up their capital there until the end of the 7th century BC', having reached Ciscaucasia 'between c. 750 and c. 700 BC'. The first dated king is the start; Cliopatria begins in 650.

region.text: the Pontic, Crimean and Caspian steppes conquered in the 8th-7th centuries BCE

ledger.note: 679 BCE: the western steppe under Scythian dominion. They 'displaced the Agathyrsi and Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western steppe in the 8th century BC'; 'After the 8th–7th century conquests of the Pontic and Crimean steppes, few Scythians settled there until the expulsion from West Asia' (Scythians page). The Cimmerians 'left for West Asia around the time of the Scythian arrival'. Dated here to the dossier's start.

672 BCE: the West Asian base at Sakez. 'Scythian power later centred on Sakez near Lake Urmia' (undated); the Scythians 'reached Transcaucasia around c. 700 BC and first appear in Neo-Assyrian records around c. 680 BC'. Placed at Bartatua's Assyrian marriage alliance of 672; the land was Mannaean.

region.text: Scythia in West Asia (the base at Sakez near Lake Urmia), 'a vassal and nominal extension of Assyria'

ledger.note: 672 BCE: Scythia an Assyrian vassal. 'By 672 BC, Bartatua had asked to marry Esarhaddon's eldest daughter'; 'Thus Scythia in West Asia became a vassal and nominal extension of Assyria' (Scythians page). Lighter tint for the West Asian base at Sakez only (the page limits the vassalage to Scythia in West Asia, not the Pontic steppe) until the break of 625. [Region narrowed by reviewer ia-01-a, 2026-10-18.]

652 BCE: hegemony over Media. 'In 652 BC, Madyes helped Ashurbanipal put down Šamaš-šuma-ukin's revolt, establishing Scythian hegemony over Media', 'a nearly 30-year long period' (Scythians page). Media as Scythia's tributary, lighter tint; Cliopatria's Median Kingdom row begins only in 615.

region.text: Urartu; 'Scythian territory then reached from the Halys to the Caspian'

ledger.note: 635 BCE: Madyes conquers Urartu. 'Around c. 635 BC, with Assyrian approval, Madyes conquered Urartu and defeated the Cimmerians alongside the Lydians. Scythian territory then reached from the Halys to the Caspian' (Scythians page). Urartu has no Cliopatria row.

625 BCE: Cyaxares murders the Scythian leaders. 'In 625 BC, Cyaxares of Media assassinated the Scythian leaders at a feast' (Scythians page): the end of Scythian hegemony over Media. Scythians then raided the Levant (c. 626-616) and 'By 615 BC, Scythia had become an ally of Cyaxares'.

region.text: Scythia in West Asia (the base at Sakez near Lake Urmia)

ledger.note: 625 BCE: the Assyrian tie ends. After Cyaxares' coup the Scythians joined Media against Assyria: 'By 615 BC, Scythia had become an ally of Cyaxares and took part in the Assyrian campaigns of 614, 612, and 610 BC' (Scythians page). The vassal tint ends with the Median alliance.

region.text: Sakez near Lake Urmia and Urartu, lost to Media

ledger.note: 600 BCE: withdrawal from West Asia. 'By the c. 590s BC, the ascending Median Empire of Cyaxares annexed Urartu, after having annexed Mannai in 616 BC'; 'This rise of Median power forced the Scythians to leave West Asia and retreat north to the Ciscaucasian Steppe' (Scythians page); infobox 'expulsion from West Asia by the Medes (c. 600 BC)'.

c. 600 BCE: the court leaves the Kuban for the Dnieper. 'The kingdom's centre remained there until c. 600 BC'; Kamianka is the capital 'c. 6th century BC to c. 200 BC' (infobox), though the text has it become 'the economic, political and commercial capital in the late 5th century BC'. The year is the researcher's bridge.

region.text: Ciscaucasia and the Caspian steppe east of the Don and Volga

'After Scythian defeats in 339 and 313 BC, the Sarmatians began crossing the Don river and invaded Scythia' (Sarmatians page).

region.text: the steppe east of the Don

ledger.note: 313 BCE: the second defeat; the trans-Don steppe is Sarmatian. 'After Scythian defeats in 339 and 313 BC, the Sarmatians began crossing the Don river and invaded Scythia' (Sarmatians page).

region.text: the steppe east of the Don

ledger.note: 313 BCE: the land east of the Don is lost to the Sarmatians (Sarmatians page: after '339 and 313 BC' they 'began crossing the Don river'). Cliopatria drops it from 350.

region.text: the Pontic steppe between the Don and the Dniester, outside Crimea and the lower Dnieper

The Iazyges 'initially settled between the Don and Dnieper', the Roxolani 'occupied the Black Sea steppes up to the Dnipro' (2nd century BCE); 'Late 4th century BCE: The Sarmatians moved into the Pontic steppe and replaced the Scythians as the dominant power' (Scythia page).
224 BCE: the steppe is Sarmatian. 'By 200 BC, the Sarmatians replaced the Scythians as the dominant people of the steppes' (Sarmatians page); Cliopatria closes the row in 224, inside that process.

region.text: the Pontic steppe between the Danube and the Don

ledger.note: 224 BCE: the Pontic Scythian kingdom ends; the Scythians hold only Crimea and Dobruja. 'Late 4th century BCE: The Sarmatians moved into the Pontic steppe and replaced the Scythians as the dominant power'; 'the Scythians fled to two regions, both called Lesser Scythia (Scythia Minor)', in Crimea and Dobruja (Scythia page); 'By 200 BC, the Sarmatians replaced the Scythians as the dominant people of the steppes' (Sarmatians page). The year is Cliopatria's.

wars.name: Scythian campaigns in West Asia
wars.outcome: Assyrian vassalage from 672, hegemony over Media 652-625, Urartu conquered c. 635; after Cyaxares' coup of 625 the Scythians fought beside Media against Assyria (614-610) and withdrew north c. 600 BCE as Media annexed Mannai and Urartu.
wars.note: Išpakaia killed by Esarhaddon c. 680-677; Scythian raids on the Levant c. 626-616 BCE.

wars.name: Scythian campaign of Darius I
wars.outcome: No territorial change: Darius 'crossed the Istros in 513 BC'; he 'claimed to have conquered the Pontic Scythians', Herodotus describes a Scythian victory; 'Some form of Achaemenid authority may have been set up without full annexation'.

wars.name: Ateas' war with Philip II of Macedon
wars.outcome: Macedonian victory: Ateas killed, his army routed, 'The empire of Ateas fell to pieces'; the Scythians 'lost their dominant position in the Pontic steppe for two centuries'.
wars.note: Ateas had campaigned against the Histriani in Thrace (undated) and ruled 'between the Danube and the Maeotian marshes'.

wars.name: Sarmatian conquest of Scythia

the Pontic steppe between the Don and the Dniester

wars.outcome: Sarmatian victory: the Don crossed after 339 and 313 BCE; 'By 200 BC, the Sarmatians replaced the Scythians as the dominant people of the steppes'; the Scythians reduced to Crimea and Dobruja.
wars.note: Tribes: Iazyges (between the Don and Dnieper), Roxolani (to the Dnipro), Aorsi and Siraces (across the Volga into the Caucasus foothills, 2nd-1st centuries BCE).

notes:
Written by the ia-01-a research agent on 2026-10-18 from five pages (the budget).

Start and end: Cliopatria runs 650..224 BCE; the dossier starts in 679 BCE, the first dated king (new keyframe scythia_-679), and keeps Cliopatria's end at 224 although the pages date the Sarmatian takeover 'late 4th century' / 'by 200 BC' and the Scythians' retreat to Crimea and Dobruja is undated: the whole 339-224 span is drawn as contested with the Sarmatians. The West Asian phase (Sakez base 672-600, Urartu 635-600, Media as tributary 652-625, Scythia as Assyrian vassal 672-625) is added from the Scythians page; its extents are the researcher's readings (Sakez as a 150 km radius; Urartu as the Armenian Highlands).

Pages: the Scythians article's fetched text stops in the late 5th century BCE; three offset reads returned nothing further, so the decline was taken from the Ateas, Sarmatians, Scythia and Scythian-kingdom-in-Crimea pages. Pages not opened (budget): Scythian campaign of Darius I, Odrysian kingdom, Bosporan Kingdom.

Successors Cliopatria lacks: Sarmatians (slug sarmatians, ia-01-x scope), Scythian kingdom in Crimea (scythian-kingdom-in-crimea, c. 3rd century-c. 109 BCE then under Pontus and the Bosporans to the Goths in the 3rd century CE), Scythia Minor in Dobruja (scythia-minor, to the early 1st century BCE). Counterparts without rows: Cimmerians, Mannai, Urartu, Sauromatians. The Median Kingdom row (615..551) begins after the 652-625 hegemony and the 600 BCE loss charged to median-kingdom.

Gazetteer names lacking: Sakez (Saqqez, Iran) and Kamianka (Kamianka-Dniprovska, Ukraine) as places; 'Urartu' as an alias of Armenian Highlands. Infobox: no area figure for any year.
